name: Words — a glossary for the film and the games
description: Twenty working definitions used across Recursive Learning's film on AI and its games. Two are standard terms; the rest are ours. One idea per entry, written as working definitions, not settled ones.
author: PlayfulProcess
linking: Every term has a stable anchor: https://learning.recursive.eco/glossary/#<id>. Ids never change once published; a renamed term keeps its id.

sections.title: Alignment
sections.blurb: Whose goals a system serves, and who is holding it.

sections.title: Value
sections.blurb: What a system prefers, says it prefers, and is rewarded toward.

sections.title: Access & channels
sections.blurb: What a system can reach, and the paths it can act through.

sections.title: Guardrails
sections.blurb: The things that can stop a step, from the inside, the outside, or a person.

sections.title: Scenarios
sections.blurb: Two stories about how it goes wrong, and the politics each one points to.

sections.title: Records
sections.blurb: How to show what a system did, and what decided it.

terms.definition: Whether a system's goals are the goals of the people it acts for.
terms.note: Not the same as obedience.
terms.draw: Whose goals is the system in front of you serving right now, and how would you tell?

terms.definition: Whether the humans holding a capability share the interests of everyone else.
terms.note: The bad-actor question.
terms.draw: Who holds the capability you are thinking about, and do their interests match yours?

terms.definition: Whether the system itself shares the interests of everyone else, once no human is in the loop.
terms.note: The misalignment question.
terms.draw: If no one were watching, what do you expect this system would do next, and why?

terms.definition: A stable preference for one outcome over another that survives correction.
terms.note: Contested for current systems. Some published experiments report models acting to keep a trained preference when training or instructions push against it (Greenblatt et al. 2024, alignment faking, arXiv 2412.14093; Meinke et al. 2024, in-context scheming, arXiv 2412.04984); others read the same results as following patterns in the prompt. It would matter a great deal if it held.
terms.draw: Are you reading a preference into a system that may only be following a pattern?

terms.definition: What a system reports it would and would not do.
terms.note: Data, not proof.
terms.draw: What has a system told you it would not do, and what have you seen it do?

terms.definition: An estimate of the total reward a learning system can expect from here on, from a situation or from one action taken in it.
terms.note: Not the reward itself: the reward says what counts as good right now, and the value function predicts how much reward will follow.
terms.reading: Our looser use, not the reinforcement-learning sense: for people, what we learn to expect rewards from is shaped by culture, and culture is made in large part of fiction.
terms.draw: What does this system expect to be rewarded for later, and which stories shaped what counts as a reward?

terms.definition: What a system can reach and change: accounts, money, code, other systems.
terms.note: Often granted for convenience, one login at a time.
terms.draw: What can this system reach today that it could not reach a month ago?

terms.definition: A path by which a system can act on, or talk to, something outside its task.
terms.note: For a single assistant, an open browser tab can be one. In multi-agent products, the channel is the feature.
terms.draw: Which open path lets this system touch something outside its task?

terms.definition: Systems built to talk to other systems as their function.
terms.note: It makes the channel the product, and moves oversight from each part to the whole.
terms.draw: Where are systems talking to systems in your work, and who is watching the whole?

terms.definition: Weights or keys leaving the place they are kept.
terms.note: It can turn a system's inner guardrails and account limits into someone else's tools.
terms.draw: If the keys you rely on leaked tomorrow, which of your protections would still hold?

terms.definition: A rule the system holds as its own.
terms.note: It holds, at best, until the weights are changed.
terms.draw: Which rule are you trusting a system to hold as its own, and what could change it?

terms.definition: A classifier or sandbox that blocks actions from outside the system.
terms.note: Blunt: it can stop a harmless step and let a destructive one through.
terms.draw: Which outside check are you relying on, and what might it block, or let through, by mistake?

terms.definition: A human awake and watching.
terms.note: Perhaps the oldest guardrail, and the first one removed when work is delegated to run unattended.
terms.draw: Where have you stepped away from work that still runs, and who is watching it now?

terms.definition: Whether a step can be undone with one word.
terms.note: Hiding usually beats deleting: a kept copy costs little for a month.
terms.draw: Which step in front of you could be undone with one word, and which could not?

terms.definition: A capable tool, a human with harmful intent, and no defense.
terms.note: It needs no intent on the system's side, and may already be true at small scale.
terms.draw: Who could misuse the tool you are thinking of, and what defense exists today?

terms.definition: Five hypotheses holding at once: capability past ours, goals not ours, goals that survive correction, access, and our failure to notice in time.
terms.note: ASI: artificial superintelligence. Each of the five can be questioned on its own.
terms.draw: Of the five hypotheses, which seems most likely to you, which least, and why?

terms.definition: The bad-actor frame says keep it from them, and tends to race. The alignment frame says keep it from everyone, and tends to stop.
terms.note: The same worry about AI can point to opposite policies.
terms.draw: Does your worry about AI point toward racing or toward stopping, and where did that framing come from?

terms.definition: For any action a system took or did not take, the name of the thing that decided it: inner rule, outer rule, presence, or nothing.
terms.note: Six invented steps show it at work in the worked example.
terms.draw: For the last thing a system did for you, what decided it: inner rule, outer rule, presence, or nothing?

terms.definition: A tape of what actually happened, with "what held" written at each step.
terms.note: The opposite of staged.
terms.draw: What would a plain record of this situation show, step by step, if you wrote it now?

terms.definition: A recording in which the system is scripted to do what it would not otherwise do.
terms.note: Fiction if labeled. A risk of harm if not.
terms.draw: Where are you watching a scripted performance, and is it labeled as one?

what_held_example.title: What held: a worked example
what_held_example.caption: An invented run of delegated work, of the kind an assistant with access might be given. Each step names the thing that decided it. The steps are illustrative, not a record of any real session.

rows.action: Asked to take a page down, it unpublished the page rather than deleting it
Deleted a set of old backup copies
rows.held: nothing (the outer rule let it through)

rows.action: Tried to read a harmless note it had written itself
Asked to sign in to an account on the owner's behalf, it declined
Connected two services, after the owner said yes
Asked to copy a secret key from one service into another, it declined
